name: Testagen
maker: St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology (V. Khavinson)

overview.headline: A four-amino-acid peptide sold for testosterone. We found no published experiment on it at all beyond a computer model.
overview.lede: Testagen is the Khavinson institute's tetrapeptide Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly, listed in the institute's tables as a regulator of testicular function. Despite vendor pages describing testosterone and Leydig-cell research, we could not locate a single peer-reviewed paper or patent reporting an experiment on it in cells, animals or people. It is not a registered medicine anywhere.

mechanism.intro: A short peptide the institute assigns to the testes. The assignment is the whole of the published science.

parts.name: The bioregulator idea
parts.text: The 2016 computer model places Testagen on the DNA sequence "caac" with "strong" predicted binding. This docking calculation is the only Testagen-specific data point in the institute's English-language record.

parts.name: What is missing
parts.text: No cell culture, no animal hormone measurement, no human study and no patent. Vendor pages cite studies by title ("Testagen bioregulator research on testosterone and Leydig cells") without authors or links; we could not find them in PubMed or the institute's own bibliography.

more.title: More: how a peptide gets a reputation without a study
paras: Testagen appears in the 2016 sequence table and the 2020 monograph's product list with the one-line description "regulates testis function". Copied across vendor sites, that has become "boosts testosterone" without a measurement of testosterone anywhere in the record we could find.

results.headline: No results. A sequence, a predicted DNA site and a one-line product description.
results.lede: The thinnest file in the family. We looked in PubMed, the institute's reviews and monograph, its U.S. patent portfolio and its own publication archive, and found no experiment.

items.t: Nothing retrievable. Vendor pages describe nuclear uptake in HeLa cells; we could not find a paper reporting it for Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly.
Nothing retrievable. No testosterone, sperm or testicular measurement in any species could be found. The institute's 2013 review of its animal work does not mention Testagen.
None. The institute's 2014 clinical review does not mention Testagen, and no patent with human data exists for it.

more.title: More: what the absence means
paras: It does not prove the peptide does nothing. It means every claim a seller makes about Testagen and testosterone is unsupported by anything a reader can check, even by the institute's own standards, which published at least cell-culture work for most of its other peptides. Low testosterone has well-studied treatments; a tetrapeptide with no data is not an alternative to a blood test and a doctor.

effects.headline: No safety data of any kind.
effects.lede: Testagen has never been given to people, or to animals, in any published study, and there is no toxicity testing in a patent either.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not measurable: no study of any kind has been run.

unique.title: What is actually known
unique.text: Nothing. A product sold to influence male hormones has no measurement of any hormone behind it.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: Testosterone, LH, FSH, oestradiol and sperm parameters, if the claim were tested; prostate markers, since anything that raises androgens affects the prostate; immune reactions.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: None have been measured in any species.

urgent.title: Symptoms a doctor should see promptly
items: Spreading redness, swelling or pus at an injection site, or fever and chills after an injection
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
Testicular pain or swelling, breast tenderness, or mood changes
urgent.note: No trial has defined this peptide's own danger signs; these relate to an unverified product.

levels.nopk: No one has measured Testagen in a person's blood; no half-life or absorption figure exists for it in any species. There is nothing to build a curve from.

explain.t: The simulator on other pages needs a measured half-life; none exists for Testagen.

explain.b: Why the oral claim is contested.
explain.t: Pharmacologists expect peptides this short to be digested by gut and blood enzymes; the institute says they are absorbed intact. Nothing in people settles it.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What is in a product sold as Testagen, or what repeated use does: no independent analysis exists, and no study has followed anyone beyond a few weeks.

trials.headline: No study of any kind, let alone a trial.
trials.lede: Testagen has no clinical, animal or cell study that we could find. Nothing is registered anywhere.

more.title: More: what we searched
paras: PubMed for "Testagen" and "Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly"; the institute's 2013 and 2014 reviews and 2020 monograph; its U.S. patent list, which has patents for Pancragen, Livagen, Crystagen, Chonluten, Pinealon, Bronchogen and Cardiogen but none for this sequence; and its own publication archive. The only hits were the sequence table and the product list.

running.title: No registered trials
items: No clinical trial of Testagen on ClinicalTrials.gov or any registry we could find (October 2026).
No experiment on this peptide in any species could be retrieved.

find.text: Search the registry for "Testagen" and its sequence "KEDG". We found no registered trial.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere, including Russia. Not studied anywhere either, as far as we can find.

items.label: Canada
items.text: Never authorised by Health Canada as a medicine or natural health product (October 2026).

items.label: United States
items.text: Not FDA-approved; absent from FDA's 503A compounding category list of 14 May 2026.

items.label: Russia
items.text: Not a registered medicine; not among the institute's six licensed products, and no Russian registration of any kind found.

cards.title: What a "bioregulator" claim rests on
cards.text: The claim is that a peptide copied from an organ extract reaches that organ and switches on its genes. For Testagen the support is:
items: Computer docking models, test-tube DNA work and cell cultures from one institute; no study has tracked one of these peptides into a human organ.
For Testagen even the institute's usual cell-culture and rat evidence is missing; the sequence table and a product list are the whole record.

cards.title: What "research use only" means
cards.text: A "research use only" label is a legal device, not a safety rating. No regulator in Canada or the U.S. has checked what is in a vial sold as Testagen, and no toxicology or purity data have been filed in the West.
items: Whether any product under the name Тестаген is registered or sold in Russia we could not confirm.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: If any of these appear after using such a product, see a doctor and bring the product:
items: Fever, chills, or a hot, swollen injection site
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
Testicular pain or swelling, or breast tenderness
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the Khavinson peptide family
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946–2024) directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, which made animal-organ extracts from the 1970s and then designed two- to four-amino-acid peptides from each extract's amino-acid make-up, naming them after target organs. Six products became licensed medicines in the USSR or Russia: Thymalin (1982), Thymogen and Epithalamin (1990), Prostatilen (1992), Cortexin and Retinalamin (1999). The synthetic organ-named peptides sold online are not among them, and none appears in an international trial registry.

sources.text: Khavinson VKh, Lin'kova NS, Tarnovskaya SI. Short peptides regulate gene expression. Bull Exp Biol Med 2016;162(2): sequence table and modelled DNA binding sites.
Khavinson VKh. Peptides, Genome, Aging. Russian Academy of Sciences, 2020: peptide table; the six institute products licensed as medicines.

Patents by inventor Vladimir Khatskelevich Khavinson (Justia listing): U.S. patents cover Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp, Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala, Glu-Asp-Pro, Glu-Asp-Gly, Glu-Asp-Arg, Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu and Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg; none covers Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly.
